title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Automotive | MPI (US)
description: On-site magnetic particle inspection for US automotive plants: dies, press parts, forgings, castings and weld fixtures. Request an MT inspection quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Automotive Plants and Suppliers in the United States
html:
Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) finds surface and near-surface cracks in ferromagnetic steel and iron parts. For US automotive plants and suppliers, Atlantis NDT examines stamping dies and press components, forgings, castings, weld fixtures and robot-cell structures on site, and reports each indication so the plant can contain, repair or scrap the part. Technicians are mobilized to the plant for shutdown weeks and scheduled downtime. To scope the work, request an MT inspection quote.

Why mag particle testing suits automotive tooling and parts

Most of what makes a vehicle, and most of what makes the machines that build it, is steel or iron. Dies, press components, forgings, gears, shafts and fixture structures are ferromagnetic, and the cracks that end their service lives start at the surface: at a radius, a keyway, a thread root or a weld toe. Magnetic particle inspection reveals those cracks in minutes, with the indication appearing directly on the part where an engineer can see it. That immediacy is why the method is a standard tool in forge shops and tool rooms.

It is also a method with a clear boundary. It requires a magnetizable material and a reasonably clean surface, and it does not see deep inside a casting or forging. Our companion pages show where the other methods take over: ultrasonic testing for automotive plants reaches internal flaws, and penetrant testing for automotive plants covers aluminum and other non-magnetic parts.

The automotive assets and parts we examine

  • Dies and tooling: forming and trimming dies, die inserts, punches and cams, where cracks start at sharp radii, screw holes and previously welded repair areas.
  • Press components: crankshafts, connecting rods, gibs, pins and tie rod threads on mechanical presses.
  • Forgings: crankshaft, camshaft, axle, steering and gear blanks, examined at the forge or at receiving inspection.
  • Ductile iron and steel castings: housings, brackets and tooling castings, with surface examination at machined faces.
  • Weld fixtures and robot-cell structures: base frames, tooling plates, clamp arms and locating pins, examined for fatigue cracks at welds and at bolted interfaces.
  • Handling gear: lifting lugs on dies, pallet frames and below-the-hook tooling used to move heavy tools; see MPI of lifting equipment.

Whose requirements apply, and the standards behind them

Automotive plants operate under a quality system, normally built on IATF 16949 plus customer-specific requirements, and that system belongs to the plant, not to us. It sets how a suspect lot is held, how records are retained and who signs a disposition. We examine to the plant's procedure or to a procedure written for the plant under Level III review, and we format the results to fit the plant's records.

Technical references vary with the part. ASTM E1444 covers the magnetic particle method for general parts, ASTM E709 is the guide to the practice, ASTM A275 sets the examination of steel forgings, MSS SP-53 covers castings and forgings for valves and fittings, and ASME Section V Article 7 sets requirements for code work. Our ASME Section V Article 7 explainer and MPI of castings and forgings page describe the method in more detail. The acceptance limits come from the purchase specification, the drawing or the customer requirement, not from the technician.

Technique choices that matter for dies, forgings and fixtures

  • Bench unit or portable yoke: a bench unit on a supplier's floor magnetizes whole parts with a head shot or coil shot; at the plant, portable yokes examine fixtures, dies in the press shop and large castings in place. We bring the equipment suited to the part and the access.
  • Wet or dry particles: wet fluorescent suspension is common for finished parts and forgings because it shows fine cracks; dry powder suits rough castings and large structures where fine sensitivity is not needed.
  • Field direction: each part is magnetized in two directions, usually circular and longitudinal, so cracks of any orientation can show.
  • Residual and continuous methods: high-retentivity steels can be examined with a residual field; low-retentivity steels need the field applied while the particles are on the part. The procedure names which one is used.
  • Surface condition: oil, scale and die lubricant block particles. Parts are cleaned to the procedure's requirement before the examination and the report records the condition.
  • Demagnetization: parts that will be machined, coated or assembled near sensitive instruments are demagnetized and the residual field is checked.

What MT finds and what it misses in automotive work

On a clean surface MT will reveal forging laps and seams, quench cracks, grinding cracks, fatigue cracks at radii and weld toes, and surface-open casting defects. It shows indications of shallow subsurface flaws in ferromagnetic steel if the field is strong enough and the flaw is close enough to the surface. It does not examine aluminum, austenitic stainless steel or other non-magnetic materials, and it does not report the depth of a crack. When depth matters, the scope should add ultrasonic testing or an engineering assessment by the plant. See MT versus PT for a short comparison of the two surface methods.

What the MT report contains

Typical contents of an automotive MT report
ItemWhat we record
Part or assetPlant, line or die number, part number, material, heat or lot where known and surface condition
ProcedureProcedure and revision, specification and edition, acceptance criterion supplied
MethodEquipment type, current type, direction of magnetization, wet or dry, visible or fluorescent, light level
ChecksYoke lifting test or bench unit verification, particle concentration, ultraviolet intensity where used
PersonnelTechnician name and level under the written practice, with the Level III who approved the procedure
FindingsLocation, length and type of each indication, accept or reject, and a marked sketch or photograph

Receiving inspection at the forge shop and the plant dock

Forgings and castings arrive with a certificate, and the certificate says what the supplier claims; magnetic particle inspection at receiving says what is actually on the surface. Typical findings on forged parts are laps folded into the surface during forging, seams carried over from the bar stock and quench cracks that appear at sharp changes of section. On castings the usual findings are cold shuts, hot tears and cracks that opened during cleaning or heat treatment. Plants that examine a sample from each lot catch a bad lot before it is machined, which is cheaper than finding the crack after the part has absorbed machining time.

A sampling plan is written into the procedure: which lots, how many parts, what happens to the rest of the lot if one part fails. We follow the plant's plan. Where there is none, we help the plant's quality engineer draft one under Level III review, then report in the same format every time so trends between lots can be seen.

Fatigue cracks in fixtures and robot-cell structures

Weld fixtures hold body panels while robots weld them, thousands of cycles a day, and they are loaded by clamps, by thermal change and by occasional collisions. Fatigue cracks usually begin at the toe of a fillet weld, at a sharp corner of a locating pad or at a bolted joint that has loosened. Because the cracks start at the surface, a portable yoke examination of the critical welds during a planned shutdown is an efficient check. The report marks which welds were examined, so the next visit repeats the same list and a growing crack can be seen rather than guessed at.

What to send for a quote

  • Parts or assets list with drawings, material and heat treatment condition
  • Specification, acceptance criterion and any customer-specific requirement
  • Lot sizes and sampling plan for supplier work, or the full list for shutdown work
  • Surface condition, coating or lubricant, and who cleans the part
  • Whether fluorescent examination is required and whether a darkened area is available
  • Lock-out requirements, access, shutdown dates, badging and the site address

Planning around plant shutdown weeks

Dies and fixtures are examined when they come out of production. Summer and year-end shutdowns are the windows where whole lines are locked out and many trades are competing for the same people and floor space, so MT on large tooling is planned weeks ahead. A die that comes off the press for maintenance can often be examined in the tool room, which is a useful alternative to shutdown weeks if the tooling is rotated on a schedule. On the supplier side, forge shops and foundries schedule examination to lot release, so we plan the visits to fit shipping.

Fluorescent work needs a darkened booth or curtained area; a tool room usually has one, a press line seldom does. Tell us early, and we will bring a portable curtain or schedule work in the tool room. Written procedures and qualification demonstrations are available through NDT technical procedure development.

Where we work in the United States for automotive

  • Toledo: forge, axle and powertrain suppliers in northwest Ohio.
  • Grand Rapids: die, fixture and component shops across west Michigan.
  • Fort Wayne: heavy truck and drivetrain manufacturing in northeast Indiana.

  • Indianapolis: transmission, forge and casting operations in central Indiana.

Training plant technicians

Plants that bring MT in-house build on MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, with the magnetic particle simulator for practice with yokes and field direction. The employer issues qualifications under its own written practice. Related material is on the manufacturing NDT training page.

Boundaries of this service

Radiography is licensed work that Atlantis does not take on in the United States, and the specialist techniques are beyond this page. We do not release product, rework parts or take over the plant's quality system; we deliver examination records. For the national overview, see magnetic particle testing and the complete MT guide.

faq.q: Can MT be used on aluminum die-cast parts?
faq.a: No. Magnetic particle inspection needs a ferromagnetic material, and aluminum does not respond. Surface cracks on aluminum castings are examined with liquid penetrant, which is covered on our automotive penetrant page.

faq.q: Do you examine dies while they are mounted in the press?
faq.a: Where access and lock-out allow, yes, using portable yokes. Dies that come off the press for maintenance are easier to examine in the tool room, and we can plan around your rotation if tooling is changed on a schedule.

faq.q: What do you need to quote MT for an automotive plant?
faq.a: Send a parts or asset list with drawings and material, the specification and acceptance criterion, lot sizes or the shutdown scope, surface condition, fluorescent requirement, lock-out and access details, dates and the site address with badging information.

faq.q: Who decides if a forging is accepted?
faq.a: The purchase specification and the plant's quality organization decide. We report each indication with its location, length and type against the supplied criterion, and the plant or the forge shop makes the release or hold decision.

faq.q: Can you inspect at our supplier's forge shop?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to the forge shop or foundry and examine lots against the purchase specification. We agree sampling, lot identification and the reporting format with you before the crew mobilizes.

faq.q: Is fluorescent MT required on automotive parts?
faq.a: Only if the specification or customer requirement says so. Fluorescent suspension is more sensitive and common on finished forgings, while dry powder is acceptable on rough castings and large structures. The procedure sets the choice.

faq.q: Does MT find cracks inside a casting?
faq.a: Only if they are close enough to the surface to disturb the magnetic field. Internal shrinkage and cracks deep in a casting are the job of ultrasonic testing, so castings with critical internal quality needs may need both methods.

faq.q: Do you demagnetize parts after examination?
faq.a: When the specification requires it. Parts headed for machining, coating or assembly near sensitive instruments are usually demagnetized and checked with a gauge, and the report records that the residual field was verified.

faq.q: Do you hold the plant's IATF 16949 certification?
faq.a: No. IATF 16949 is the plant's quality system, and we work inside it by following your procedures and record formats. For its own management system Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, which is a different thing.
